section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
question: In information theory, what does the entropy $H(p)$ of a distribution measure?
options: The number of outcomes with nonzero probability under $p$
The extra cost of encoding $p$'s data with a model $q$
The largest probability any single outcome of $p$ receives
The average surprise (information content) per draw from $p$
explanation: Entropy is the expected surprisal of a distribution: on average, how much information each draw from $p$ carries. The extra cost of using a model $q$ instead of $p$ is the KL divergence, not entropy. Entropy depends on the whole shape of $p$, not just its peak or support size.

section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
question: What does the cross-entropy $H(p, q)$ represent when data truly comes from $p$ and a model $q$ is used?
options: The average surprisal of $q$'s own samples, scored under $q$ itself
The probability that $p$ and $q$ pick the same outcome on one draw
The average cost of scoring/encoding $p$'s data using $q$'s probabilities
The symmetric distance between $p$ and $q$, the same in either argument order
explanation: Cross-entropy is the average surprisal you incur when outcomes happen with frequencies $p$ but are scored with $-\log q(x)$. The surprisal of $q$'s own samples under $q$ would be $H(q)$. It is not symmetric and is not a probability of agreement.

section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
question: Why is cross-entropy central to training language models?
options: The LM training loss is cross-entropy between the model's predicted distribution and the true next token
It measures how large a vocabulary the model needs to cover the training corpus without unknowns
It replaces the softmax layer at the output, turning raw logits directly into next-token predictions
It is used only to evaluate models after training; the training loss itself is mean squared error
explanation: Every language model is trained by minimizing cross-entropy between its predicted next-token distribution $q$ and the true next token. It is the training loss itself, not merely an evaluation metric, and it works alongside (not instead of) softmax.

section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
question: Cross-entropy decomposes into two parts. Which description of them is correct?
options: Two KL divergences, one from model to truth and one from truth to model, added together
The model's entropy plus the data's entropy, both reducible by training on more data
An irreducible part (the data's entropy) plus a reducible part (the KL gap between model and truth)
A reducible part (the data's entropy) plus an irreducible part (the KL gap between the model and truth)
explanation: $H(p, q) = H(p) + \mathrm{KL}(p \parallel q)$. $H(p)$ depends only on the data and no model can lower it; the KL term is the model's mismatch and can be driven toward zero. The tempting swap gets it backwards: entropy of the data is the fixed part.

question: What is the core intuition information theory starts from about surprise?
options: A common event carries more information because it is observed more often
A rare event is more surprising and carries more information than a common one
All events carry equal information regardless of probability
Surprise depends only on how many outcomes are possible, not their probabilities
explanation: The founding idea is that rare outcomes are more informative: seeing rain in a desert teaches you a lot, seeing sun teaches you almost nothing. So the measure of surprise must be large when $p(x)$ is small, and it depends on each outcome's probability, not just the count of outcomes.

question: How is the surprisal (information content) of an outcome $x$ with probability $p(x)$ defined?
options: $\log p(x)$, equivalently $-\log \frac{1}{p(x)}$
$-\log p(x)$, equivalently $\log \frac{1}{p(x)}$
$1 - p(x)$, the probability that $x$ does not occur
$-p(x) \log p(x)$, the term $x$ adds to the entropy
explanation: Surprisal is $-\log p(x) = \log(1/p(x))$: large when $p(x)$ is near 0 and zero when $p(x) = 1$. Plain $\log p(x)$ is non-positive, so it has the wrong sign. $-p(x)\log p(x)$ is one term of the entropy sum, not the surprisal of a single outcome.

question: What is the surprisal $-\log p(x)$ of an outcome that is certain, $p(x) = 1$?
options: $\log 2$, one bit of information per observation
$+\infty$, because it happens on every single draw
0, because a certain event carries no surprise
1, the maximum possible surprisal for any event
explanation: $-\log 1 = 0$. A certain event teaches you nothing when it happens, so it carries zero information. Infinite surprisal is the opposite extreme, reached as $p(x) \to 0$.

question: Why is the surprisal $-\log p(x)$ always non-negative?
options: Because the logarithm of any positive number is positive, and $p(x)$ is always positive
Because probabilities exceed 1 in log space, so $\log p(x) \ge 0$ before the sign is applied
Because $p(x) \le 1$ makes $\log p(x) \le 0$, and the minus sign flips it to $\ge 0$
Because surprisal is defined with an absolute value, $|\log p(x)|$, rather than a minus sign
explanation: Probabilities lie in $[0, 1]$, and the log of a number at most 1 is at most 0. The leading minus sign turns that non-positive number into a non-negative one. Logs are not always positive (e.g. $\ln 0.5 < 0$), and no absolute value is involved.

question: Surprisal measured with $\log_2$ is in bits. What unit results from using the natural log $\ln$?
options: Nats
Hartleys per bit
Bits
Bans
explanation: Using $\ln$ gives nats; $\log_2$ gives bits. Bits count yes/no questions needed to pin down an outcome. The two units differ by the constant factor $\ln 2 \approx 0.6931$.

question: By what factor do an information quantity in nats and the same quantity in bits differ?
options: $\ln 2 \approx 0.6931$, since $\log_2 x = \ln x / \ln 2$
$e \approx 2.718$, since nats use base $e$ and bits base 2
$2$, since bits use base 2 and $\log_2 x = 2 \ln x$
$\log_{10} 2 \approx 0.301$, since $\log_2 x = \log_{10} x / 2$
explanation: Change of base gives $\log_2 x = \ln x / \ln 2$, so the value in bits equals the value in nats divided by $\ln 2 \approx 0.6931$. It is not a factor of 2 or $e$; the conversion constant is the natural log of the base 2.

question: Why does a course that matches PyTorch by hand compute information quantities in nats rather than bits?
options: Bits cannot represent fractional information, so nats are needed for non-integer entropies
Nats are always smaller numbers than bits, so they avoid overflow in long float32 sums
PyTorch converts everything to bits internally, so working in nats is needed to undo that conversion
PyTorch's log, softmax and cross_entropy all use the natural log, so nats match its outputs exactly
explanation: PyTorch's `log`, `softmax`, and `cross_entropy` use the natural log, so working in nats makes hand computations agree with PyTorch to the last decimal. Bits can be fractional, and PyTorch does not convert to bits.

question: An entropy is quoted as some value in bits. How do you convert a value in nats to bits?
options: Divide the nats value by 2, the base of bits
Divide the nats value by $\ln 2 \approx 0.6931$
Multiply the nats value by $\ln 2 \approx 0.6931$
Take $2$ raised to the nats value, $2^{H}$
explanation: Since $\log_2 x = \ln x / \ln 2$, a value in nats divided by $0.6931$ (equivalently multiplied by $1.4427$) gives bits. Multiplying by $\ln 2$ goes the other way (bits to nats). Exponentiating is unrelated to unit conversion.

section: 2. Entropy: the average surprisal of a distribution
question: How is the entropy $H(p)$ defined in terms of surprisal?
options: The expected surprisal: $H(p) = E_{x\sim p}[-\log p(x)] = -\sum_x p(x)\log p(x)$
The maximum surprisal: $H(p) = \max_x -\log p(x)$, the rarest outcome's cost
The unweighted sum of surprisals: $H(p) = -\sum_x \log p(x)$ over all outcomes
The surprisal of the most likely outcome only: $H(p) = -\log \max_x p(x)$
explanation: Entropy weights each outcome's surprisal $-\log p(x)$ by its probability $p(x)$ and sums: the expectation as a probability-weighted sum. An unweighted sum would treat rare and common outcomes equally, and the max or most-likely-only versions ignore most of the distribution.

section: 2. Entropy: the average surprisal of a distribution
question: In $H(p) = -\sum_x p(x)\log p(x)$, what roles does $p(x)$ play?
options: It is only the argument of the log (the surprisal); the weights over outcomes are uniform
It is a normalizing constant that makes the sum equal 1, playing no role inside the log
It is both the weight (how often $x$ occurs) and the argument of the log (the surprisal)
It is only the weight (how often $x$ occurs); the log uses a separate model distribution
explanation: In entropy the same distribution supplies both the weights and the logs. That is exactly what distinguishes it from cross-entropy, where the weights come from $p$ but the logs come from a model $q$.

section: 2. Entropy: the average surprisal of a distribution
question: What convention is used for the term $0 \log 0$ in entropy, and what does it mean?
options: $0 \log 0 = 0$: an impossible outcome contributes no surprise
$0 \log 0 = 1$: an impossible outcome contributes one nat
$0 \log 0 = -\infty$: an impossible outcome makes entropy infinite
$0 \log 0$ is undefined, so such distributions have no entropy
explanation: By convention $0 \log 0 = 0$, justified by the limit $p\log p \to 0$ as $p \to 0$. An outcome that never happens is never paid for, so it adds nothing to the average surprise. Distributions with zero entries still have well-defined entropy.

section: 2. Entropy: the average surprisal of a distribution
question: Which distribution over $K$ outcomes has the maximum entropy, and what is that maximum?
options: The uniform distribution, with entropy $\log K$ nats
A one-hot distribution, with entropy $\log K$ nats
Any distribution with full support, with entropy 1 nat
The uniform distribution, with entropy $K$ nats
explanation: Uniform is maximally uncertain (every outcome equally surprising) and reaches the ceiling $\log K$. A one-hot distribution is the opposite, with entropy 0. The ceiling is $\log K$, not $K$; $K$ itself appears after exponentiating, as perplexity.

section: 2. Entropy: the average surprisal of a distribution
question: What is the entropy of a distribution that puts probability 1 on a single outcome?
options: $+\infty$, because the other outcomes have zero probability
1 nat, the minimum nonzero entropy
$\log K$, because there are $K$ possible outcomes
Exactly 0, because there is no uncertainty
explanation: A one-hot distribution has $H = -(1\cdot\log 1) = 0$; the zero entries drop out by $0\log 0 = 0$. A sure thing carries no surprise. Zero-probability outcomes do not make entropy infinite.

section: 2. Entropy: the average surprisal of a distribution
question: The fact that the maximum entropy over $K$ outcomes is $\log K$ underlies which later quantity?
options: The number of attention heads, which scales with $\log K$ of the vocabulary
Perplexity, whose worst (uniform) value equals the vocabulary size
The KL penalty coefficient in RLHF, which is set to $\log K$ by default
The learning rate schedule, whose peak is tied to $\log K$ of the outputs
explanation: The $\log K$ ceiling is why a uniform model has loss $\log V$ and perplexity $\exp(\log V) = V$. That is the perplexity connection; it is unrelated to learning rates, attention heads, or RLHF penalties.

question: For $p = (0.5, 0.25, 0.25)$, the entropy is about 1.0397 nats, while the uniform distribution over 3 outcomes has $\ln 3 \approx 1.0986$ nats. Why is $p$'s entropy lower?
options: Because $p$ is peakier (favors one outcome), so it carries less surprise per draw than uniform
Because entropy is always lower for distributions that repeat a probability value, like 0.25 twice
Because $p$ has fewer possible outcomes than the uniform distribution it is compared with
Because $p$'s entropy was computed in bits while $\ln 3$ is in nats, so they are not comparable
explanation: Uniform is the maximum-entropy distribution, so any distribution that favors some outcome has lower entropy. Both distributions are over 3 outcomes and both values are in nats. Repeated probabilities are not the reason; non-uniformity is.

section: 3. Cross-entropy: encoding p's data with q's beliefs
question: How is the cross-entropy $H(p, q)$ written as a sum?
options: $H(p, q) = -\sum_x q(x)\log q(x)$
$H(p, q) = \sum_x p(x)\log \frac{p(x)}{q(x)}$
$H(p, q) = -\sum_x p(x)\log q(x)$
$H(p, q) = -\sum_x q(x)\log p(x)$
explanation: Cross-entropy weights by the true $p(x)$ and takes the log of the model $q(x)$. Swapping weights and logs computes a different quantity. $-\sum q\log q$ is the model's own entropy, and $\sum p\log(p/q)$ is the KL divergence.

section: 3. Cross-entropy: encoding p's data with q's beliefs
question: In cross-entropy $H(p, q)$, why are the weights the true probabilities $p(x)$ while the logs use $q(x)$?
options: Because $p$ is the model's prediction and $q$ is the empirical data, so the data supplies the logs
Because the logs of $p$ are unknown in practice, so $q$ stands in for them and $p$ only serves to normalize the sum
Because $q$ must always be uniform, so taking its log adds the same constant $\log K$ to every term
Because $p(x)$ is how often each outcome really happens, and $q$ is the distribution used to score/predict it
explanation: Each time outcome $x$ occurs you are charged $-\log q(x)$, and $x$ occurs with frequency $p(x)$. So the frequencies are $p$ and the charge uses $q$. There is no requirement that $q$ be uniform, and the weights are not the model's.

section: 3. Cross-entropy: encoding p's data with q's beliefs
question: When is the cross-entropy $H(p, q)$ minimized over $q$, and what is its minimum value?
options: When $q$ is one-hot, where it equals 0
When $q$ is uniform, where it equals $\log K$
When $q = 1 - p$, where it equals the KL divergence
When $q = p$, where it equals the entropy $H(p)$
explanation: Cross-entropy equals $H(p)$ exactly when the model matches the truth and is strictly larger for any mismatch. So 'make $q$ match $p$' and 'minimize $H(p,q)$' are the same goal, which is why it is the training loss. A uniform or one-hot $q$ is optimal only if $p$ happens to be that distribution.

section: 3.1 Worked example: cross-entropy of q against p
question: With $p = (0.5, 0.25, 0.25)$ and $q = (0.25, 0.25, 0.5)$, $H(p,q) \approx 1.2130 > H(p) \approx 1.0397$. What does the excess of about 0.1733 nats represent?
options: The entropy of $q$, the model's own uncertainty about the next outcome
The KL divergence $\mathrm{KL}(p \parallel q)$, the cost of using the wrong distribution
The entropy of the uniform distribution minus $H(p)$, the headroom remaining in $p$
A rounding error from using natural logs instead of base-2 logs in the sums
explanation: The amount by which cross-entropy exceeds the entropy is exactly $\mathrm{KL}(p \parallel q)$: extra average surprisal paid for encoding with $q$ instead of $p$. It is not $H(q)$ and not a numerical artifact.

section: 4. KL divergence: how far q is from p
question: How is the KL divergence $\mathrm{KL}(p \parallel q)$ defined?
options: $\sum_x p(x) |\log p(x) - \log q(x)|$
$\sum_x q(x)\log \frac{p(x)}{q(x)}$
$\sum_x p(x)\log \frac{p(x)}{q(x)}$
$\sum_x p(x)\log \frac{q(x)}{p(x)}$
explanation: KL is the $p$-weighted average of the log-ratio $\log(p/q)$: $E_{x\sim p}[\log(p(x)/q(x))]$. Weighting by $q$ gives a different quantity. The absolute-difference sum is total variation, and $-\sum p \log q$ is cross-entropy.

section: 4. KL divergence: how far q is from p
question: In words, what does $\mathrm{KL}(p \parallel q)$ measure?
options: The probability that a sample drawn from $q$ actually came from $p$
The average surprisal of draws from the true distribution $p$ under $p$
The total surprisal of $q$ summed over all outcomes, unweighted
The extra average surprisal paid for using $q$ instead of the true $p$
explanation: KL measures how much worse $q$ does than the truth: the excess average surprisal over the optimum $H(p)$. The average surprisal of $p$ is the entropy itself. KL is not a probability.

section: 4. KL divergence: how far q is from p
question: Which property states that $\mathrm{KL}(p \parallel q) \ge 0$ with equality iff $q = p$?
options: The chain rule of probability
Bayes' theorem
Gibbs' inequality
The triangle inequality
explanation: Non-negativity of KL, with equality exactly when the distributions match, is Gibbs' inequality. KL does not satisfy the triangle inequality in general (it is not a metric). Bayes and the chain rule are unrelated.

section: 4. KL divergence: how far q is from p
question: Why is the KL divergence not a true distance (metric)?
options: Because it is only defined when both $p$ and $q$ are uniform distributions over $K$ outcomes
Because it is asymmetric: $\mathrm{KL}(p \parallel q) \ne \mathrm{KL}(q \parallel p)$ in general
Because it is zero for some pairs of different distributions, so $\mathrm{KL} = 0$ does not imply $p = q$
Because it can be negative, so $\mathrm{KL}(p \parallel q) < 0$ happens for some pairs
explanation: KL is non-negative and zero only when $q = p$, but swapping the arguments generally changes its value, so it fails symmetry. It is never negative and is defined for general distributions.

section: 4. KL divergence: how far q is from p
question: In $\mathrm{KL}(p \parallel q)$, which distribution supplies the weights?
options: The second argument, $q$ (the model distribution)
Both $p$ and $q$, averaged together as $(p+q)/2$
The first argument, $p$ (the true distribution)
Neither; the weights are uniform over outcomes
explanation: The first argument provides the weights: $\mathrm{KL}(p \parallel q) = \sum_x p(x)\log(p(x)/q(x))$. Reversing the order changes which distribution weights the log-ratios, which is why the order matters.

question: In computing $\mathrm{KL}(p \parallel q)$, some individual terms $p(x)\log(p(x)/q(x))$ can be negative. What must be true of the total?
options: The total equals zero whenever any term is negative
The total must be negative if any term is negative
The total is undefined if any term is negative
The total is still $\ge 0$, by Gibbs' inequality
explanation: Terms where $q(x) > p(x)$ have a negative log-ratio, but the $p$-weighted sum is always non-negative. For example, with $p = (0.5, 0.25, 0.25)$, $q = (0.25, 0.25, 0.5)$ one term is $-0.173$ yet the total is $+0.173$.

section: 5. The identity H(p, q) = H(p) + KL(p || q)
question: Which identity ties together cross-entropy, entropy and KL divergence?
options: $H(p, q) = H(p) - \mathrm{KL}(p \parallel q)$
$H(p, q) = H(p) + \mathrm{KL}(p \parallel q)$
$H(p, q) = H(p) \cdot \mathrm{KL}(p \parallel q)$
$H(p, q) = H(q) + \mathrm{KL}(q \parallel p)$
explanation: Cross-entropy equals entropy plus KL. Since KL is non-negative, this means $H(p,q) \ge H(p)$. A minus sign would allow the loss to go below the entropy, which cannot happen; the other forms swap or misuse the distributions.

section: 5. The identity H(p, q) = H(p) + KL(p || q)
question: The derivation of $H(p,q) = H(p) + \mathrm{KL}(p\parallel q)$ starts by rewriting $\log q(x)$. Which rewrite is used?
options: $\log q(x) = \log p(x) - \log \frac{p(x)}{q(x)}$
$\log q(x) = \log p(x) \cdot \log q(x)$
$\log q(x) = \frac{\log p(x)}{\log(p(x)/q(x))}$
$\log q(x) = \log p(x) + \log \frac{p(x)}{q(x)}$
explanation: From $\log(p/q) = \log p - \log q$, rearranging gives $\log q = \log p - \log(p/q)$. With a plus sign the identity fails (check $p = 0.5$, $q = 0.25$). This split separates 'the best possible log-probability' from 'the gap'.

section: 5. The identity H(p, q) = H(p) + KL(p || q)
question: The rewrite $\log q(x) = \log p(x) - \log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}$ comes from which basic rule?
options: $\log(a + b) = \log a + \log b$, then rearranged once
$e^{\log a} = a$, applied to the ratio $p/q$
$\log \frac{a}{b} = \log a - \log b$, rearranged
$\log(a^b) = a \log b$, applied to the ratio
explanation: It is the quotient rule for logs applied to $p(x)/q(x)$, then rearranged to isolate $\log q(x)$. $\log(a+b) = \log a + \log b$ is false in general, and the power and exponent rules are not what this step uses.

section: 5. The identity H(p, q) = H(p) + KL(p || q)
question: Why is it useful to split $\log q(x)$ into $\log p(x)$ and $\log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}$?
options: It makes the cross-entropy symmetric in $p$ and $q$, so the order of the two arguments no longer matters
The first piece depends only on the truth (becomes $H(p)$) and the second measures the model's gap (becomes KL)
It removes the need to know $p$ during training, since only the second piece involves the data
Both pieces depend only on the model, so they can be optimized separately with two different losses
explanation: $\log p(x)$ involves only the true distribution and becomes the entropy; $\log(p/q)$ is zero when $q(x) = p(x)$ and becomes the KL. This separates the irreducible part from the part the model controls. It does not make anything symmetric.

section: 5. The identity H(p, q) = H(p) + KL(p || q)
question: In $H(p,q) = H(p) + \mathrm{KL}(p \parallel q)$, why does minimizing cross-entropy over the model amount to minimizing KL?
options: Because $H(p)$ is always zero for real data, leaving only the KL term
Because $H(p)$ is fixed by the data and the optimizer cannot change it
Because KL and cross-entropy are always equal, whatever $p$ happens to be
Because the optimizer minimizes $H(p)$ first and then turns to KL
explanation: The entropy term depends only on the data, so it is a constant with respect to the model's parameters; all change in the loss comes from the KL term. $H(p)$ is zero only for one-hot targets, and cross-entropy equals KL only in that case.

section: 5. The identity H(p, q) = H(p) + KL(p || q)
question: In the decomposition of the language-modeling loss, what does the entropy term $H(p)$ represent?
options: The irreducible uncertainty of the language itself, which no model can remove
The uncertainty introduced by the tokenizer alone, which a better vocabulary removes
The regularization penalty on the model weights, which shrinks as training proceeds
The model's own mistakes on the data, which training gradually drives toward zero
explanation: $H(p)$ is a property of the data: genuine uncertainty about what comes next. No model can do better on average. The model's fault is the KL term, which is zero exactly when $q = p$.

section: 5.1 Verify the whole thing in Python
question: In PyTorch, which code computes the cross-entropy $H(p,q)$ for probability tensors `p` and `q`?
options: `-(q * p.log()).sum()`
`-(p * p.log()).sum()`
`-(p * q.log()).sum()`
explanation: Cross-entropy uses weights `p` and logs of `q`. `-(q * p.log()).sum()` swaps them, `-(p * p.log()).sum()` is the entropy of `p`, and `(p * (p/q).log()).sum()` is $\mathrm{KL}(p\parallel q)$.

section: 5.1 Verify the whole thing in Python
question: In PyTorch, what does `.log()` on a tensor compute?
options: The natural logarithm $\ln$, so results are in nats
The log-softmax along the last dimension of the tensor
The base-2 logarithm, so results are in bits
The base-10 logarithm, so results are in hartleys
explanation: Tensor `.log()` is the natural log. That is why the course works in nats: hand calculations then match PyTorch outputs. It is not base 2 or 10, and it is not log-softmax.

section: 5.1 Verify the whole thing in Python
question: When `Hp + KL` is computed in float64 PyTorch and compared with `Hpq`, what is observed?
options: They differ by a small amount, because the KL term is only an approximation
They differ by exactly $\ln 2$, because of the change from bits to nats
`Hp + KL` is always slightly larger than `Hpq` due to rounding
They agree to machine precision, confirming the identity numerically
explanation: The identity $H(p,q) = H(p) + \mathrm{KL}(p\parallel q)$ is exact, so the numbers match to machine precision. There is no unit mismatch (all natural logs) and KL is computed exactly, not approximated.

section: 6. Why cross-entropy against a one-hot target is the LM training signal
question: When training a language model, what is the 'true' distribution $p$ at a single position?
options: Uniform over the vocabulary, since every token is a possible next token
One-hot: probability 1 on the observed next token and 0 elsewhere
The unigram frequency of each token in the training corpus
The model's own softmax output, treated as a soft target
explanation: At each position the true next token is a single known token $t$, so $p$ is one-hot on $t$. It is not the model's output, not uniform, and not corpus-wide frequencies.

section: 6. Why cross-entropy against a one-hot target is the LM training signal
question: When the true distribution is one-hot on token $t$, what does the cross-entropy $H(p, q)$ reduce to?
options: $-\log q(t)$, the negative log-probability of the true token
$1 - q(t)$, the probability mass placed on the wrong tokens
$-\sum_x \log q(x)$, summed over every token in the vocabulary
$-\log q(t) - \sum_{x\ne t} \log(1 - q(x))$
explanation: Every term with $p(x) = 0$ vanishes, leaving only the $x = t$ term with weight 1: $-\log q(t)$. Wrong tokens do not appear at all. $1 - q(t)$ is not a log loss, and the extra terms belong to a binary per-token loss, not categorical cross-entropy.

section: 6. Why cross-entropy against a one-hot target is the LM training signal
question: Minimizing cross-entropy against one-hot next-token targets is equivalent to what?
options: Maximizing the log-likelihood of the observed text
Minimizing the entropy of the model's predictions
Minimizing the KL divergence from the model to the uniform distribution
Maximizing the entropy of the data
explanation: With one-hot targets the per-token cross-entropy is $-\log q(t)$, the negative log-likelihood of the observed token. Summing over positions gives the negative log-likelihood of the text, so minimizing it is maximum likelihood. It does not directly target entropy or uniformity.

section: 6. Why cross-entropy against a one-hot target is the LM training signal
question: For a one-hot target $p$, what does the identity $H(p,q) = H(p) + \mathrm{KL}(p\parallel q)$ become?
options: $H(p,q) = H(q)$, since the model's entropy dominates
$H(p,q) = H(p)$, since $\mathrm{KL} = 0$ for one-hot $p$
$H(p,q) = \log V + \mathrm{KL}(p\parallel q)$, since $H(p) = \log V$
$H(p,q) = \mathrm{KL}(p \parallel q)$, since $H(p) = 0$
explanation: A one-hot distribution has zero entropy, so for one-hot targets the cross-entropy loss equals the KL divergence: the model's entire loss is its distance from the truth. KL is zero only if the model is exactly one-hot on the correct token.

section: 6. Why cross-entropy against a one-hot target is the LM training signal
question: In cross-entropy against a one-hot target, how is the model told to distribute probability among the wrong tokens?
options: The loss requires all wrong tokens to have exactly zero probability, enforced term by term
Each wrong token gets an explicit penalty proportional to its probability in the loss
Wrong tokens are pushed toward a uniform distribution by a separate entropy term
It is not told explicitly; only $q(t)$ appears, and softmax handles the rest implicitly
explanation: Only the true token's probability enters $-\log q(t)$. The wrong tokens are pushed down implicitly because softmax ties all probabilities together: raising $q(t)$ forces the others to shrink. There is no separate term for them in the loss.

section: 6. Why cross-entropy against a one-hot target is the LM training signal
question: What single scalar per position is the language-model loss?
options: The raw probability the model assigns to the correct next token, unlogged
The entropy of the model's predicted distribution at that position
The negative log-probability the model assigns to the correct next token
The difference between the largest logit and the correct token's logit
explanation: The per-position LM loss is $-\log q(t)$. Using the raw probability would not be a log loss. The model's entropy is a different quantity, and the logit gap is not the loss itself (the loss is logsumexp minus the true logit).

question: Your hand-computed entropy differs from PyTorch's by a factor of about 0.6931. What is the most likely cause?
options: Using float32 instead of float64, which loses about 30% of the value
Weighting by $q$ instead of $p$, which swaps the roles of truth and model
Mixing bits and nats (using $\log_2$ instead of $\ln$ or vice versa)
Forgetting to normalize the distribution so that it sums to 1
explanation: A factor of exactly $\ln 2 \approx 0.6931$ is the signature of a unit mismatch between bits and nats. Wrong weighting or missing normalization give unrelated errors, and float32 vs float64 differences are tiny, not a constant factor.

question: What goes wrong if you compute $-\sum_x q(x)\log p(x)$ when you meant the cross-entropy $H(p,q)$?
options: Weights and logs are swapped, so it computes a different quantity entirely
Nothing; cross-entropy is symmetric in $p$ and $q$, so the order is free
It gives the same value as $H(p,q)$, but measured in bits instead of nats
It gives the KL divergence $\mathrm{KL}(p \parallel q)$ instead of cross-entropy
explanation: In $H(p,q)$ the weights are the true $p(x)$ and the logs are the model $q(x)$. Swapping them computes $H(q,p)$, which is generally different; cross-entropy is not symmetric. It is not a unit change and is not the KL.

question: Why does the asymmetry of KL divergence matter later in a language-model curriculum?
options: It forces the learning rate to be decreased over the course of training
It determines the vocabulary size the tokenizer is allowed to use
Argument order matters in RLHF/DPO, where KL penalties are used
It makes the softmax non-invertible, so logits cannot be recovered
explanation: KL's asymmetry means the order of arguments encodes which distribution supplies the weights, and this matters in preference-tuning methods like RLHF and DPO. It has nothing to do with vocabulary size, softmax invertibility, or learning rate schedules.

question: What happens to the loss if the model assigns $q(x) = 0$ to a token that actually occurs ($p(x) > 0$)?
options: The term is dropped by the convention $0 \log 0 = 0$
The loss equals $\log V$, the uniform-model value
The loss is $+\infty$, because $-\log 0 = +\infty$
The loss is 0 for that token, since it contributes nothing
explanation: The convention $0\log 0 = 0$ applies only when the weight $p(x)$ is zero. Here the weight is positive and the log's argument is zero, giving an infinite loss. That is why models must never output exactly zero probability.

question: In entropy and cross-entropy, what decides whether a zero probability is harmless or catastrophic?
options: Whether the distribution has more than two outcomes (harmless) or only two outcomes (catastrophic)
Whether the zero occurs at the first position of the vector (harmless) or the last position (catastrophic)
Whether the computation is done in nats (harmless) or in bits, where $\log_2 0$ is not defined at all (catastrophic)
Whether the zero is in the weight $p(x)$ (harmless) or inside the log, $q(x)$, with $p(x) > 0$ (catastrophic)
explanation: A zero weight $p(x) = 0$ makes its term vanish; a zero inside the log with nonzero weight gives $+\infty$. Position in the vector, units, and number of outcomes do not change this.

question: Why is the convention $0 \log 0 = 0$ mathematically justified?
options: Because any finite number times infinity is zero, so $0 \cdot (-\infty) = 0$
Because probabilities of zero are rounded up to $10^{-8}$ before taking logs
Because $\lim_{p\to 0^+} p\log p = 0$: $p$ shrinks faster than $\log p$ grows
Because $\log 0 = 0$ by definition, so the whole term vanishes
explanation: As $p$ gets smaller, e.g. $0.1\ln 0.1 = -0.230$, $0.01\ln 0.01 = -0.046$, $10^{-6}\ln 10^{-6} \approx -0.0000138$, the product tends to 0. $\log 0$ is $-\infty$, not 0, and $0\times\infty$ is not generally zero; the limit justifies the convention.

question: What is the intuitive meaning of $0 \log 0 = 0$ in entropy?
options: An outcome that never happens is never paid for, so it adds no average surprise
An impossible outcome adds exactly one nat, the cost of ruling it out
An impossible outcome is maximally surprising, so it dominates the sum
An impossible outcome doubles the entropy contributed by all the other outcomes
explanation: Its weight is zero, so the term vanishes. For example $p = (0.5, 0.5, 0)$ has entropy $\ln 2 \approx 0.693$, exactly a fair coin; the impossible outcome contributes nothing.

question: In cross-entropy, if a token has true probability $p(x) = 0$, how much does the model's $q(x)$ for that token directly affect the score?
options: Not at all, since the term has weight 0
It adds $-\log q(x)$ to the loss
It adds $q(x)$ to the loss
It makes the loss infinite unless $q(x) = 0$
explanation: A token with zero true probability gets weight 0 in $-\sum p\log q$, so its $q(x)$ does not appear in the score. It matters only indirectly: probability given to it is taken away from tokens that do occur.

question: What does `-(p * p.log()).sum()` return in PyTorch for `p = torch.tensor([0.5, 0.5, 0.0])`, and why?
options: `0.0`, because the zero entry zeroes out the whole product before the sum
`inf`, because `log(0) = -inf` and the minus sign flips it to `+inf`
`0.6931`, because PyTorch applies the $0\log 0 = 0$ convention automatically in `log`
`nan`, because `log(0) = -inf` and `0 * -inf` is `nan` in IEEE floating point
explanation: The computer evaluates `log(0) = -inf` first, then `0 * -inf`, which is `nan` in IEEE floating point. One `nan` makes the sum `nan`. The convention $0\log 0 = 0$ exists on paper, not in hardware.

question: Which PyTorch function computes $x \log y$ but returns exactly 0 when $x = 0$, implementing $0\log 0 = 0$?
options: `torch.log1p`
`torch.nan_to_num`
`torch.xlogy`
`torch.logsumexp`
explanation: `torch.xlogy(x, y)` computes `x * log(y)` and returns 0 wherever `x == 0`, so `-torch.xlogy(p, p).sum()` gives the correct entropy. `log1p` computes $\log(1+x)$, `logsumexp` is a reduction, and `nan_to_num` would only patch the symptom after the fact.

question: Besides `torch.xlogy`, how can you avoid the `nan` when computing entropy of a vector containing zeros?
options: Replace the zeros with $-\infty$ so the log is well defined
Drop the zero entries first, e.g. sum only over `p[p > 0]`
Add 1 to every entry before taking the log, then subtract 1
Take the log in base 2 instead, which handles zero entries
explanation: Masking to `p[p > 0]` removes exactly the terms that are 0 by convention, giving the correct value. Adding 1 changes the result, changing base does not fix $\log 0$, and $-\infty$ entries are not valid probabilities.

question: Why does a `nan` in a computed entropy or loss matter so much during training?
options: It is automatically replaced by zero, so it only slightly biases the loss
It halts training with an exception immediately
It only affects logging, not the gradients
One `nan` makes the whole sum `nan` and poisons every gradient
explanation: Any `nan` term propagates through the sum, making the loss `nan`, and backpropagation then fills gradients with `nan`, corrupting the weights. It is not silently replaced and does not necessarily raise an exception.

question: A one-hot target written as a probability vector, `target`, is used in `-(target * target.log()).sum()`. What bug appears?
options: A shape error, because one-hot vectors cannot be logged
`nan`, because every non-target entry is $0 \times \log 0$
No bug; the result is exactly 0
An infinite loss, because the target entry is $\log 1$
explanation: Each zero entry gives `0 * log(0) = 0 * -inf = nan`, so the sum is `nan` even though the true answer is 0. The target entry is $1\cdot\log 1 = 0$, which is fine; the zeros are the problem.

question: Why can no convention rescue the term $-p(x)\log q(x)$ when $q(x) = 0$ but $p(x) > 0$?
options: Because the $0\log 0$ convention only applies when the computation is carried out in bits, not nats
The weight is nonzero, so the term is genuinely $+\infty$: the model called the token impossible and it occurred
Because conventions are only allowed in entropy, and cross-entropy is defined without any special cases
Because PyTorch reserves the $0\log 0$ rule for `xlogy`, and plain `log` cannot apply it to this term
explanation: With $p(x) > 0$ the term is $-p(x)\times(-\infty) = +\infty$, an infinite loss meaning infinite surprise. The $0\log 0$ convention needs a zero weight, which is absent here. Units are irrelevant.

question: The true next token is `cat`. Compare the loss if the model gives $q(\text{cat}) = 0$ vs $q(\text{cat}) = 0.001$.
options: Infinite vs about 6.9 nats; the second is large but finite, so gradients can still pull it up
Zero vs about 6.9 nats; a zero probability is skipped by the $0\log 0$ convention
Both are infinite, since any probability below $10^{-2}$ underflows the logarithm in float32 arithmetic
Both are about 6.9 nats, since the loss saturates once the probability is that small
explanation: $-\ln 0 = +\infty$ while $-\ln 0.001 \approx 6.9$. A finite loss gives a usable gradient that pushes the true token's probability up; an infinite one does not.

question: Why does softmax mathematically guarantee $q_i > 0$ for every token?
options: Because softmax clips every output to at least $10^{-8}$ before normalizing the distribution
Because softmax adds a small epsilon to every output so that no single probability can ever be exactly zero
Because $e^{z}$ is strictly positive for every real $z$, and the denominator is a positive sum
Because logits are always positive, so their ratio to the total is positive as well
explanation: $q_i = e^{z_i}/\sum_j e^{z_j}$ and $e^{z}$ is positive for all real $z$, so every $q_i$ is positive. Logits can be negative, and standard softmax adds no epsilon or clipping.

question: When can softmax output exactly 0 in practice despite the mathematical guarantee?
options: Never; softmax outputs are always strictly positive in float32 and float64 alike
Only when all logits are equal, so every output collapses to the same tiny value
Only when a logit is exactly 0, because $e^0$ is then dropped from the sum
When $e^{z_i}$ underflows in floating point, e.g. $e^{-200}$ in float32 rounds to 0
explanation: Float32 has a smallest representable value; $e^{-200} \approx 10^{-87}$ is below it and rounds to exactly 0. A logit of 0 gives $e^0 = 1$, and equal logits give a uniform distribution, neither of which is zero.

question: For logits `[0.0, -200.0]` in float32, what do `softmax(...).log()` and `log_softmax(...)` return?
options: Both return `[0, -inf]`
Both return `[0, -200]`
explanation: Two-step `softmax` then `log` first forms $e^{-200}$, which underflows to 0, then $\log 0 = -\infty$. `log_softmax` computes $z_i - \log\sum_j e^{z_j}$ directly and returns the finite $-200$.

question: What is the recommended fix for the softmax-then-log underflow problem?
options: Compute $\log q_i = z_i - \log\sum_j e^{z_j}$ directly with `log_softmax`, never forming tiny $q_i$
Divide the logits by a large temperature before softmax, so no probability gets small enough to underflow
Add $10^{-8}$ to the softmax output before taking the log, which keeps every value finite and exact
Compute the softmax in float16, whose extra precision keeps tiny probabilities above zero
explanation: Log-softmax never forms the tiny probability, so it cannot underflow to 0. Adding an epsilon changes the result and hides the issue; float16 has less range, not more; changing temperature changes the model's distribution.

question: Why does `torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy` take raw logits instead of probabilities?
options: Because it needs the raw logits to infer the vocabulary size from the size of the last dimension
Because logits take less memory than probabilities, since they are stored in float16
Because probabilities are not differentiable once they have passed through a softmax
It computes log-softmax internally, avoiding underflow from forming tiny probabilities
explanation: `cross_entropy` applies a numerically stable log-softmax to the logits, so for logits `[0, -200]` with target 1 it returns 200, not `inf`. Probabilities are differentiable and have the same memory footprint; the reason is numerical stability.

question: `F.cross_entropy(z, t)` is literally equivalent to which composition?
options: `nll_loss(softmax(z), t)`
`-softmax(z)[t].log().mean()` computed in two steps
`log_softmax(nll_loss(z, t))`
`nll_loss(log_softmax(z), t)`
explanation: `cross_entropy` computes log-probabilities with `log_softmax`, then `nll_loss` picks $-\log q_t$. Using `softmax` instead of `log_softmax` would not be a log-probability, and the explicit two-step softmax-then-log version reintroduces underflow.

question: In the stable log-sum-exp $m + \log\sum_j e^{z_j - m}$, what is $m$?
options: The mean logit in the row, $\frac{1}{V}\sum_j z_j$
The minimum logit in the row, $\min_j z_j$
The maximum logit in the row, $\max_j z_j$
The logit of the true token, $z_t$
explanation: Subtracting the max $m$ makes the largest shifted exponent $e^0 = 1$ and all others at most 1. That prevents overflow and keeps the sum at least 1. The mean or minimum does not give these guarantees.

question: Why does $m + \log\sum_j e^{z_j - m}$ equal $\log\sum_j e^{z_j}$ exactly?
options: Because the max term dominates the sum and the remaining terms are dropped as negligible
Because $\log$ is linear, so $\log\sum_j e^{z_j} = \sum_j \log e^{z_j - m} + m$
Because $e^{z_j - m} = e^{z_j} - e^m$, so the shift cancels inside the sum
Factoring $e^m$ out of the sum: $\log(e^m \sum_j e^{z_j - m}) = m + \log\sum_j e^{z_j - m}$
explanation: Each $e^{z_j} = e^m e^{z_j - m}$, so the sum factors as $e^m \sum_j e^{z_j-m}$, and the log of a product splits into $m$ plus the rest. It is exact, not an approximation that drops terms.

question: In stable log-softmax on logits $(0, -200)$, $e^{-200}$ still underflows to 0. Why is that harmless here?
options: It is harmless because the underflowed term is multiplied by zero later in the loss computation
It is only added to the max term $e^0 = 1$, so the sum is off by about $10^{-87}$, a negligible error
It is not harmless at all; the loss becomes infinite as soon as any term underflows to zero
It is harmless because PyTorch switches to float64 automatically whenever an exponential underflows to zero
explanation: The tiny exponential only appears as an addend next to $e^0 = 1$, so the computed sum is 1 instead of $1 + 10^{-87}$. Meanwhile $z_1 = -200$ enters the final subtraction as an ordinary number, giving $\log q_1 = -200$ and loss 200.

question: Why can the log-sum-exp in a max-shifted log-softmax never be $-\infty$?
options: The sum always contains the max term $e^0 = 1$, so it is at least 1 and its log is at least 0
Because each exponential is rounded up to $10^{-38}$, the smallest float32, before it is summed
Because the log is only ever applied to the max logit, never to the full sum of exponentials
Because logits are clipped to be non-negative, so every exponential in the sum is at least 1
explanation: After subtracting the max, at least one shifted logit is exactly 0, contributing $e^0 = 1$. The sum is therefore $\ge 1$, so the log-sum-exp offset is $\ge m$ and finite. No clipping or rounding up is involved.

question: Besides avoiding $\log 0$, what other numerical problem does subtracting the max logit prevent?
options: Negative probabilities, which large negative logits would otherwise produce
Overflow: large logits like 1000 would make $e^{1000} = \text{inf}$ in float32
Division by zero, which happens whenever all the logits in a row are equal
Loss of gradient for the true token when its logit is the largest one
explanation: With $z = (1000, 800)$, the naive $e^{1000}$ is `inf`. Shifted by the max, the exponentials are $e^0$ and $e^{-200}$, giving log-sum-exp 1000 and $\log q_2 = -200$. Equal logits never cause division by zero, and softmax never yields negative probabilities.

question: Why does subtracting the max logit from every logit not change the softmax output?
options: Softmax is invariant to adding the same constant to all logits; only differences matter
Because the shift is undone by a later multiplication by $e^m$ inside the loss function
Because the max logit is always zero after training, so subtracting it changes nothing
It does change the output slightly, but the change stays within float32 tolerance
explanation: Shifting all logits by a constant multiplies numerator and denominator by the same factor, which cancels. So the probabilities are exactly the same; the max logit need not be zero originally.

question: If a model's $q$ is uniform over 2 outcomes, what is its cross-entropy against any true distribution $p$ over those outcomes?
options: 0 nats, since a uniform model is never surprised
It depends on $p$ and can be any non-negative value
$\ln 2 \approx 0.6931$ nats, regardless of $p$
$H(p)$ nats, since cross-entropy then equals entropy
explanation: When $q$ is uniform both logs equal $\ln 0.5$, and the weights $p(x)$ sum to 1, so $H(p,q) = -\ln 0.5 = \ln 2$. In general a uniform model over $K$ outcomes always costs $\ln K$.

question: Given $H(p)$ and $H(p,q)$ for a true distribution $p$ and model $q$, how can $\mathrm{KL}(p\parallel q)$ be obtained without summing log-ratios?
options: $\mathrm{KL}(p\parallel q) = H(p,q) + H(p)$
$\mathrm{KL}(p\parallel q) = H(p,q) - H(p)$
$\mathrm{KL}(p\parallel q) = H(p) - H(p,q)$
$\mathrm{KL}(p\parallel q) = H(p,q) / H(p)$
explanation: Rearranging $H(p,q) = H(p) + \mathrm{KL}(p\parallel q)$ gives KL as cross-entropy minus entropy. $H(p) - H(p,q)$ would be non-positive, contradicting KL's non-negativity.

question: Term by term, how do entropy $H(p)$ and cross-entropy $H(p,q)$ differ?
options: Entropy sums over every outcome, while cross-entropy takes a maximum over the outcomes instead
Entropy uses natural logs throughout, while cross-entropy uses base-2 logs for every term
Entropy weights each term by the model $q$, while cross-entropy weights each term by the true $p$
Both weight by the true $p$; entropy takes logs of $p$, cross-entropy takes logs of the model $q$
explanation: Both are probability-weighted sums of negative log-probabilities with weights from $p$. The difference is whose log-probabilities appear: $p$'s in entropy, $q$'s in cross-entropy. They are equal exactly when $q = p$, and otherwise $H(p,q) > H(p)$.

question: With one-hot targets, what does driving the cross-entropy loss to 0 require of the model?
options: Its logits must all be exactly zero, so that every token receives the same probability
Its $q$ must exactly match the one-hot target, putting probability 1 on the true token
Its distribution must become uniform, spreading probability evenly over the vocabulary
Its entropy must equal $\log V$, the maximum possible uncertainty over the vocabulary
explanation: For one-hot $p$, loss $= \mathrm{KL}(p\parallel q) = -\log q(t)$, which is 0 only when $q(t) = 1$. Uniform predictions or zero logits give loss $\log V$, the opposite of perfect.

question: A hand-computed entropy is 0.693 but a textbook says 1.0 for the same distribution. What is the explanation?
options: The hand calculation forgot the minus sign, which flips and shrinks the result
The textbook uses bits and the hand calculation uses nats; $0.693 = 1.0 \times \ln 2$
The hand calculation applied the $0\log 0 = 0$ convention incorrectly to a zero entry
The textbook used a different distribution with more outcomes and hence more entropy
explanation: $0.693 \approx \ln 2$, the bits-to-nats factor, so 1 bit equals 0.693 nats. A missing minus sign would produce a negative value, not a scaled one. To convert nats to bits multiply by $1/\ln 2 \approx 1.4427$.
